terminology pass 2026-09-28 (GLOSSARY.md): "almost linear" -> a linear classifier on the encoded states already reaches 0.943; "linear rule" -> linear classifier; "leading discriminants" -> two leading Fisher discriminant directions; "local / wiki" -> this reproduction / reported; "revised / original" -> phase on |b(m)> / phase on |m+1>.

2026-09-29 (speaker: "what is LDA? ... What was the best classical model?"): LDA here meant linear discriminant analysis (Fisher's linear discriminant), not latent Dirichlet allocation; it is used only to choose the 2D plane of the left figure. The axis labels now read "Fisher discriminant z1/z2". Caption removed; the figure now labels itself (legend: grey = reported, blue = this reproduction; panel title "four classes"). The RBF SVM bar was added and the trained-model bar changed from 0.903 (§4.3, seeds 0-4) to the held-out 0.890 (§3). (Superseded in the second round: legend and reproduction bars removed; panel title now "test accuracy, 4 digits"; bar colours slate / gold / grey.)

2026-09-29, second round (speaker: "just use reported one"): the bar chart (title "test accuracy, 4 digits"; slate = linear classifier, gold = trained model with CC, grey = classical references, none of them a digit colour of the planes) now shows reported values only: 0.773 / 0.943 (§2.4), 0.890 (§3), 0.964 / 0.978 (§0.1). Removed: the "this reproduction" bars (0.754 / 0.927) and the raw-x bar (0.664, a local number; the vault reports no linear classifier on the raw 40 features of this four-class task: §1, §2.4, §4.2 and §10 checked, and mnist1d-eda.md's logistic 0.329 is the ten-class task), and with them the legend. The two decision-region panels stay as an illustration of the geometry only; they come from the local reproduction and no accuracy of theirs is shown or spoken.

Speaker note: left, an illustration of the geometry: the 411 test signals projected on the two leading Fisher discriminant directions (shrinkage linear discriminant analysis on the training signals), raw x against the encoded states with the phase on |b(m)>, with the decision regions of a linear classifier fitted in that plane. The encoded classes separate into four regions; the raw features overlap. (These panels were computed here from the documented untrained encoding, not taken from the reported runs; quote no accuracy from them.) Conversely every linear classifier defines a POVM, E_c = I/4 + mu (W_c - W-bar) with 0 < mu << 1 (App. A), so the bound is attained, but by a joint POVM on all three encoded states (one 12-qubit measurement) and only with nearly uniform output probabilities. Three separate QPUs without communication instead multiply their Born-rule distributions, which loses accuracy through calibration (§1, App. A); on these untrained states the product of per-window optimal POVMs reaches 0.774 (§2.4). Right, reported four-class test accuracies: the linear classifier on the untrained encoded states, 0.773 with the phase on |m+1> and 0.943 with it on |b(m)> (§2.4); the trained model with CC on seeds 3-7 (0.890, §3); tuned RBF SVM and the best classical classifier on all 40 features, a kernel logistic regression whose shift-aware kernel is a sum of RBF kernels over the cyclic width-5 sub-windows, chosen on validation data among 2330 classical models (§0.1).

Figure: 3. wiki/code/lm-260929-animations/fig_linear.py, re-run 2026-09-29 on the local CPU (second re-run the same day: the bar chart plots only the reported constants WIKI_LIN_ORIG, WIKI_LIN_REV, MODEL_COMM, SVM_RBF, CLASSICAL_BEST; the planes are unchanged; every computed number unchanged; third re-run after review: bar title "test accuracy, 4 digits" and slate / gold / grey bar colours, planes pixel-identical, _verify() passed), deterministic (no random draws except sklearn's deterministic lbfgs). Encoding: dqml_style cyclic contiguous windows (0-13, 14-27, 27-39 plus 0; dqml-quantum-stage.md §2 "Slicings"), untrained revised or original state preparation with percentile_scale_offset() (1st-99th training percentiles of |X_m| onto [0, pi], the slot-encoder convention of dqml-quantum-stage.md §1), constant tree angles pi/2. Split: first 1325 of the 1589 four-class training signals = training, last 264 = validation (C chosen on validation from 10^-3..10^3), 411 test. Features: 256 independent reals of each 16 x 16 rho (diag, Re and Im upper triangle), constant features dropped, standardised. Local test accuracies (provenance of the planes only, shown nowhere on the slide): raw 40 features 0.664 (C = 0.0316); original encoding 0.754 (C = 0.00316); revised encoding 0.927 (C = 0.0316). 2D rules in the Fisher-discriminant (LDA) planes: 0.672 (raw), 0.917 (revised). _verify() checks the cyclic windows, the rho parametrisation, that the fitted rule equals sum_b Tr[W_c^(b) rho_b] + beta_c with Hermitian W_c, that E_c = 1/4 + mu (W_c - mean W) is positive with the same argmax on all 411 test signals (mu = 0.00797, max |P_c - 1/4| = 0.070: uncalibrated, App. A), that changing the constant tree angles (pi/2 -> 1.0) leaves the test accuracy identical, and (added 2026-09-29) that the bar chart shows exactly 0.773, 0.943, 0.890, 0.964, 0.978 and none of the local accuracies. Fourth re-run 2026-09-29 (speaker: "What is Best classical model?"): the 0.978 bar label "best classical" became "kernel logistic regression (shift-aware)" (constant CLASSICAL_BEST_LABEL, checked in _verify()); only that label's pixels changed, the planes are pixel-identical, _verify() passed.

Reproduction gap (was an EDIT-FORWARD; resolved 2026-09-29 by plotting reported values only): the local reproduction behind the planes gives 0.927 (phase on |b(m)>) and 0.754 (phase on |m+1>), 1.6 to 1.9 points below the reported 0.943 and 0.773; the difference between the two encodings is reproduced (+17.3 points locally against +17.0 reported). The local run uses the documented slot-encoder scale (1st-99th percentile onto [0, pi], offset at the 1st percentile), but the untrained scale/offset initialisation of the reported runs is not in the vault (~/DQML, phys-embed-layout); the level depends strongly on it (dqml_style.default_scale, pi / 95th percentile, offset 0: 0.849 and 0.662). The constant tree angles are irrelevant for this bound (standardisation removes them). The split sizes match the vault (1325 / 264 / 411, dqml-physics-results.md §0.1), but which training signals were held out for validation is not recorded there. Since the planes carry no numbers, the gap does not affect anything shown.

W_c in E_c collects the three templates (acting on the joint 12-qubit product state) and the bias beta_c (as beta_c Tr rho), App. A; W-bar is the class average.

EDIT-FORWARD: why 0.943 (linear bound) > 0.890 (trained model): the product of Born-rule distributions loses accuracy through calibration (§1, App. A); the bound is attained only by a nearly uniform POVM.

src: dqml-physics-results.md §8, Phase 2g bullet (revised encoding; source phys-phase2g/README.md §7): single 12-qubit QCNN 0.805 ± 0.076 against 0.865 without and 0.908 with communication, 0 of 3 wins in both comparisons, circuit parameters 1656 against 1128 and 1188, 0.60 nats of entanglement entropy between the data blocks (22 % of the maximum after the first circuit layer), linear-classifier accuracy of its own trained encoding 0.864 against 0.946; Phase 2 bullet (original encoding: 1-6 points below three QPUs without communication for every window type); paragraph after the bullets (differs in circuit, pooling and readout; reference = quantum channel with the same crossing budget, decided 2026-09-26). Single-QPU model definition: §0.2 "Other variants" (one QPU holding all 3n qubits, same product-state encoding, one global brick-wall circuit, pooling down to one 2-qubit readout).

terminology pass 2026-09-28 (GLOSSARY.md): "one large QPU" -> monolithic QPU; "clean reference" -> matched baseline; "quantum channel with the same crossing budget" -> QC at the same communication cost and circuit location; "data blocks" -> feature blocks' registers; "linearly readable" -> linear-classifier accuracy.

Speaker note: "0.864 vs 0.946" = linear-classifier accuracy on the monolithic QCNN's own trained encoded states against that of the distributed model (§8). The monolithic QPU holds all 12 qubits with the same encoding, one brick-wall circuit over all of them and pooling layers down to one 2-qubit readout: a standard QCNN (§0.2). CC (2->1) = classical communication, 2 senders -> 1 receiver. "entanglement between the blocks" = 0.60 nats of entanglement entropy between the registers of the three feature blocks (22 % of the maximum after the first circuit layer). The matched baseline is quantum communication (QC): the pooled qubits are sent to the receiving QPU instead of being measured, at the same communication cost and circuit location as the classical message bits; the deck lists it as an open item (bits vs qubits), not as a result. With the original encoding the monolithic QCNN was also the least accurate model, 1-6 points below NC (§8 Phase 2).

2026-09-29 integration (second round): visible "0.60 nats of entanglement" -> "entanglement across the feature blocks" (no nats on visible slides; the 0.60-nats entanglement entropy stays in the speaker note), and "Matched: quantum communication (QC)" dropped, because the QC comparison slide (57-quantum-channel.md) was removed and the deck no longer shows QC results.

Speaker note: the additive model is the best classical model whose log-probability is a sum of per-block terms (naive-Bayes-like, the classical product of experts); the joint model sees all 40 features at once (here the kernel logistic regression with the shift-aware kernel, chosen on validation data among 2330 classical models). What the additive model loses is class information found only in combinations of blocks, which only communication can carry. With contiguous blocks that is 0.7 points, yet communication adds 1.1 to 3.1 points to our model, depending on the seeds: 1.1 points on seeds 3-7, not used for model selection (NC 0.878 -> 0.890, the values of the accuracy slide); 2.3 points on seeds 0-7 (0.873 -> 0.896); 3.1 points on seeds 0-4 (0.872 -> 0.903, the topology slide). Each is at least the 0.7-point additive loss. And even with communication (0.890 to 0.903) our model stays below the additive classical model (0.971), so this gain need not use combinations across blocks (our reading). With permuted features there are 8.7 points to gain from combinations, but a block is no longer a piece of the signal: a feature partition of one classical vector is an artificial way to create a distributed task, and it removes the reason for the Fourier (DFT) encoding.

2026-09-29 (speaker, second review: "interpret it without using CE or D_add"): the D_add formula, the D_add column (0.021 / 0.224 nats) and the bullet "communication lowers CE by 0.17 to 0.19 nats (8 to 9 x D_add), mostly offsetting the bounded confidence of Born-rule outputs" were removed; the slide now argues in accuracy only. The cross-entropy provenance is kept below for reference.

Speaker note: this answers "we want more than a classification task, right?": yes. On MNIST-1D the label is mostly local: a classical additive per-block model already reaches 0.971 with contiguous blocks (0.891 permuted), so communication has little to carry and adds only a few points, and a classical model on all 40 features, a kernel logistic regression with a shift-aware kernel chosen on validation data among 2330 classical models, reaches 0.978, above every quantum model. In an inherently distributed task each QPU holds its own input and the answer is a joint function f(x, y) of them, so without communication the referee can only guess; the figure of merit becomes the communication cost (message size) needed for a given worst-case error. Communication complexity offers a whole menu of such f with known quantum and classical costs: equality, Hamming distance, disjointness, hidden matching, vector in subspace, and inner product mod 2 as a counterexample with no advantage (next slide). A machine-learning flavoured variant: two QPUs each receive a whole signal and the receiving QPU decides "same digit?" (a verification task); no advantage is proven for that one. Equality is itself a binary classification of the pair (x, y): what changes is not "classification or not" but that the inputs sit on different QPUs and the figure of merit becomes message size at a given worst-case error instead of test accuracy. The "now" column is contiguous blocks; with permuted features communication adds 5.7 to 7.5 points (§4.3), but a block is then no longer a piece of the signal.

Speaker note (clip): Alice and Bob each send a fingerprint |h_x> = (1/sqrt m) sum_i (-1)^{E_i(x)} |i>, built from an error-correcting code E whose distinct code words differ in many positions, so |<h_x|h_y>| <= delta for x != y. The referee runs the SWAP test and answers "equal" with probability (1 + |<h_x|h_y>|^2)/2: 1 if x = y, at most (1 + delta^2)/2 otherwise; k copies push the error down. The clip uses a toy code with 16 amplitudes (4 qubits), not the paper's: one flipped bit gives <h_x|h_y> = 0.25 and P(0) = 0.53, where P(0) is the probability of "equal".

2026-09-29 round 2 (user on the protocol slide: "there are more operations more than =="): the proposal column now names a family of joint functions f(x, y) instead of equality alone; the "quantum advantage" row says "proven for some f, not for all" (inner product mod 2 has none, Cleve et al. 1998, see 64a); "message size at a given error" became "... worst-case error"; the fingerprint clip moved here from 64a (as the worked example for one f) so that 64a can hold the table of functions. Fixer pass: "each QPU holds" in the proposal column changed from "its own input, x or y" to "senders: x or y; receiver: none", consistent with the SMP referee (no input) on 64a (verifier).

The mapping onto our QPUs is our proposal, not the papers'.

Speaker note (table): costs are the communication in qubits (quantum) or bits (classical); n = input length in bits (for the subspace problem, the dimension of x, a unit vector in R^n; y is a subspace of dimension n/2, promise x in y or in its orthogonal complement). Hamming distance: d fixed. Disjointness: x, y read as subsets of {1..n}, f = 1 iff there is no i with x_i = y_i = 1; the first quantum protocol, O(sqrt n log n), is Buhrman, Cleve, Wigderson 1998, the matching Omega(sqrt n) lower bound is Razborov 2003. Boolean hidden matching: introduced (with the relational hidden matching problem) by Bar-Yossef, Jayram, Kerenidis 2004; the one-way separation for a Boolean variant is Gavinsky et al. 2007. Vector in subspace: quantum one-way, classical lower bound for two-way protocols. SMP = simultaneous message passing: each party sends one message to a referee who holds no input; one-way = one message from Alice to Bob; two-way = interactive. All rows are bounded error (correct with probability >= 2/3 on every input), costs up to constant factors. Promise problems (partial functions) are defined only on inputs that satisfy a promise; in this table the exponential separations for one-way protocols are of this kind, and hidden matching started as a relation (several valid outputs). Equality and Hamming distance: the separation needs "no shared randomness"; with a shared random key equality costs O(1) classical bits. Inner product mod 2 is the counterexample: Theta(n) qubits even with prior entanglement, so not every joint function benefits (for exact protocols, entanglement halves the cost to ceil(n/2) qubits by superdense coding and no further; with bounded error it stays Omega(n), Cleve et al. eqs. 2-3). Not in the table: the distributed Deutsch-Jozsa problem (promise: x = y or Hamming distance n/2) needs O(log n) qubits exactly but Omega(n) bits for exact (zero-error) classical protocols (Buhrman, Cleve, Wigderson 1998, Theorem 1.7); with bounded error, classical O(log n) bits suffice, so it separates only exact protocols. Also: for almost all functions, quantum fingerprinting is exponentially worse than classical deterministic SMP (Gavinsky, Kempe, de Wolf, CCC 2006): fingerprints help for special functions such as equality and bounded Hamming distance.

Speaker note (architecture and first target): our default topology, two senders -> one receiver, has the shape of the SMP model once the receiving QPU gets no input of its own (in the model the referee holds no input; today our receiving QPU encodes its own feature block). Equality is the natural first target: (i) its separation is in the SMP model, which matches this topology without interaction; (ii) the referee is small: each sender sends a k-qubit fingerprint |h_x> = (1/sqrt m) sum_i (-1)^{E_i(x)} |i>, and the SWAP test needs 2k + 1 qubits (two registers and one ancilla, paper eq. 3 and Fig. 1), answering "equal" with probability (1 + |<h_x|h_y>|^2)/2; (iii) the same SWAP test, repeated on k copies, estimates the overlap |<u|v>| (Yao 2003, Lemma 1), which is how Yao's Hamming-distance protocol works, so Hamming distance is the natural second step. The disjointness protocols are interactive: every Grover query becomes a round trip of O(log n) qubits (Buhrman, Cleve, Wigderson, Theorem 2.1: t queries give a t(2 log2 N + 4)-qubit protocol), hence a two-way topology. With CC each sender transmits message bits; with QC it transmits its qubits. No communication (NC) gives the chance level. What we would learn: whether training finds fingerprint-like codes and a SWAP-test-like referee, and whether trained classical messages stay above the sqrt(n) scaling on worst-case inputs. Classical baseline: an unrestricted classical b-bit encoder of x (or the Theta(sqrt n) bound itself), not only our threshold-bit CC, because the paper's classical bound is for unrestricted classical senders while our CC sends a threshold of a K-shot estimate of the sender's encoded state; a CC-vs-QC gap measured with our CC alone could reflect the restricted sender, not the communication bound.

Speaker note (caveat, our analysis, not in the paper as stated): CC = classical communication, QC = quantum communication (the pooled qubits are sent). Trained parameters act as a shared key, so average test accuracy can hide the gap. For a fixed input distribution, averaging the paper's shared-key protocol over the key shows that some fixed key has average error at most the protocol's worst-case error (Yao's minimax principle; Kushilevitz and Nisan, Communication Complexity, 1997). A trained classical model has fixed parameters chosen with knowledge of the training distribution, so it can reach low average error with O(1) bits per sender; the Theta(sqrt n) bound concerns worst-case inputs. The paper itself notes that "for every fixed key value, there are distinct inputs x and y on which the protocol gives the incorrect output 1" (p. 1). Hence: evaluate on adversarially chosen pairs (worst case), not only on a fixed test set.

src (equality row): 1. raw/papers/buhrman2001quantum/buhrman2001quantum.pdf. SMP model, Alice and Bob "are not permitted to communicate with one another directly. Rather they each send a message to a third party, called the referee" (p. 1). Shared random key: "the fingerprints need only be of constant length if we allow a small probability of error" (p. 1). Without a shared key: "Ambainis [4] proved that fingerprints of O(sqrt n) bits suffice ... Newman and Szegedy [7] proved the above is optimal" (pp. 1-2). Theorem 1: "O(log2(n)) qubits of communication [contrasting with Theta(sqrt n) bits classically]". Fingerprint eq. (5), Theorem 2: log2(n) + O(log2(1/delta)) qubits, |<h_x|h_y>| <= delta. SWAP test eq. (3), Fig. 1: "equal" (outcome 0) with probability (1 + |<phi|psi>|^2)/2; one-sided error (1 + delta^2)/2. Logarithmic length is also necessary without a shared key (p. 3).

src: scope of the equality row (kept from the previous version, verifier 2026-09-29): the Theta(sqrt n) vs O(log n) separation holds in the simultaneous message passing model without a shared key (abstract; Theorem 1, p. 2); in the ordinary two-party model with private coins equality costs only O(log n) classical bits (Buhrman-Cleve-Wigderson 1998, Theorem 1.1: C(EQ) in O(log N); Klartag-Regev 2011, p. 1), so the model is named in the table.

src (Hamming distance row): A. C.-C. Yao, "On the power of quantum fingerprinting", STOC 2003, pp. 77-81 (read 2026-09-29, cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spr04/cos598A/Stoc03.pdf): HAM_n^(d)(x, y) = 1 iff Hamming distance <= d; Theorem 2: R^{||,pub}(HAM^(d)) = O(d^2); Corollary: "For any fixed d, Q^{||}(HAM_n^(d)) = O(log n)" (SMP, quantum, no shared randomness); Theorem 1: R^{||,pub}(f) = O(1) implies Q^{||}(f) = O(log n). Classical Theta(sqrt n) without shared randomness is our combination of cited results: upper O(d^2 sqrt n) from Yao's remark "R^{||}(f_n) = O(R^{||,pub}(f_n) n^{1/2})" (citing Babai-Kimmel, Kushilevitz-Nisan, Newman-Szegedy) with Theorem 2; lower Omega(sqrt n) because equality on n/(d+1) bits reduces to HAM^(d) on n bits by repeating every bit d+1 times (distinct inputs then differ in >= d+1 positions), and equality needs Omega(sqrt n) (Newman-Szegedy). Yao's Lemma 1: k SWAP tests estimate |<u|v>| with Pr{|error| > beta} < 2 exp(-k beta^4 / 32).

src (disjointness row): Buhrman, Cleve, Wigderson, "Quantum vs. classical communication and computation", STOC 1998 (arXiv quant-ph/9802040, read 2026-09-29): Theorem 1.6 Q(DISJ) in O(sqrt N log N); Theorem 1.3 [Kalyanasundaram-Schnitger 1987/1992, Razborov 1990/1992] C(DISJ) in Omega(N), bounded error, two-party interactive. Aaronson and Ambainis, "Quantum search of spatial regions", FOCS 2003; Theory of Computing 1, 47-79 (2005), arXiv quant-ph/0303041: "an O(sqrt(n))-qubit communication protocol for the disjointness problem, which ... matches a lower bound of Razborov". Razborov, "Quantum communication complexity of symmetric predicates", Izvestiya Math. 67, 145-159 (2003), arXiv quant-ph/0204025: Omega(sqrt n) for disjointness, with or without prior entanglement. Classical: Kalyanasundaram and Schnitger, SIAM J. Discrete Math. 5, 545-557 (1992); Razborov, Theor. Comput. Sci. 106, 385-390 (1992).

src (hidden matching row): Bar-Yossef, Jayram, Kerenidis, "Exponential separation of quantum and classical one-way communication complexity", STOC 2004 (SIAM J. Comput. 38, 366-384 (2008)): Hidden Matching is a relation (Alice x in {0,1}^n, Bob a perfect matching M, output (i, j, x_i XOR x_j) with (i, j) in M), one quantum message of log n qubits vs about sqrt n classical one-way bits; also separates quantum SMP from classical SMP with public coins (as summarised in Gavinsky et al. 2007, p. 2, and Klartag-Regev 2011, p. 2; the BJK paper itself was not accessible, ACM 403). Gavinsky, Kempe, Kerenidis, Raz, de Wolf, "Exponential separations for one-way quantum communication complexity, with applications to cryptography", STOC 2007, pp. 516-525 (arXiv quant-ph/0611209, read 2026-09-29; Theorem 2 as in the arXiv/journal version, SIAM J. Comput. 38(5), 1695-1708 (2008), Crossref doi 10.1137/070706550; the arXiv version supersedes quant-ph/0607173 and quant-ph/0607174): partial Boolean function alpha-Partial Matching (Theorem 2 assumes alpha in (0, 1/4] "for technical reasons"; the original Boolean Hidden Matching of BJK04 is alpha = 1/2, a perfect matching, where "by communicating the parity of x in one bit, Alice can give Bob one bit of information about z"; the conference version "had two different communication problems": Remarks after Theorem 2, arXiv quant-ph/0611209 p. 4, re-read by the fixer 2026-09-29), "a variant of the Boolean Hidden Matching Problem"; Theorem 2: classical bounded-error one-way R1 = Theta(sqrt(n/alpha)), quantum one-way Q1 = O(log(n)/alpha); alpha = 1/4 gives O(log n) qubits vs Omega(sqrt n) bits. Classical two-way protocols solve it with O(log n) bits (Klartag-Regev p. 2), so the separation is one-way only.

src (subspace row): Klartag and Regev, "Quantum one-way communication can be exponentially stronger than classical communication", STOC 2011, pp. 31-40 (arXiv 1009.3640, read 2026-09-29): Vector in Subspace Problem, Alice a unit vector u in R^n, Bob a subspace H of dimension n/2, promise u in H or u in H-perp; quantum one-way ceil(log2 n) qubits (Bob measures (H, H-perp), no error); classical randomized bounded-error two-way lower bound Omega(n^{1/3}); classical O(sqrt n) upper bound. The problem was first defined by Kremer (master's thesis, Hebrew University, 1995; Klartag-Regev §4, "first defined by Kremer [Kre95]", and p. 2) and also described by Raz (STOC 1999), whose two-round quantum protocol gave the first bounded-error exponential separation.

src (inner product row): Cleve, van Dam, Nielsen, Tapp, "Quantum entanglement and the communication complexity of the inner product function", QCQC 1998, LNCS 1509, 61-74 (arXiv quant-ph/9708019, read 2026-09-29), eqs. (2)-(5): with prior entanglement Q*_0(IP) = ceil(n/2), Q*_eps(IP) >= (1/2)(1 - 2 eps)^2 n - 1/2, C*_0(IP) = n. Classical randomized Omega(n): Chor and Goldreich, SIAM J. Comput. 17, 230 (1988) (Theorem 1.2 of Buhrman-Cleve-Wigderson 1998). Hence Theta(n) both ways: "no advantage" = no asymptotic advantage.

src (not on the slide): distributed Deutsch-Jozsa, EQ'(f, g) = 1 if Hamming distance 0, 0 if 2^(n-1) (N = 2^n bits): Q_0(EQ') in O(log N), C_0(EQ'), C_0E(EQ') in Omega(N) (Buhrman-Cleve-Wigderson 1998 Theorem 1.7; the quantum protocol can be one-way); bounded-error classical C(EQ) in O(log N) (their Theorem 1.1). Gavinsky, Kempe, de Wolf, "Strengths and weaknesses of quantum fingerprinting", CCC 2006, pp. 288-295 (arXiv quant-ph/0603173): "for almost all functions, quantum fingerprinting protocols are exponentially worse than classical deterministic SMP protocols".

src (bullets): mapping onto our QPUs, "first target" and "worst-case error vs message size" are our proposal, not the papers'. SWAP test on 2k + 1 qubits: paper eq. (3), Fig. 1.

Speaker note: one message to take home. If asked what comes next (the removed list, speaker-only): (1) an inherently distributed task, equality by quantum fingerprinting, measuring worst-case error against message size for classical (CC) against quantum communication (QC); (2) classical messages of increasing precision in place of the qubit: one bit, <Z>, the Bloch vector, the full reduced state (the last reproduces QC for our product readout, so the question is the cost in classical bits and copies); (3) other networks: remove message edges at random and retrain (cf. lottery tickets, found by magnitude pruning, Frankle and Carbin), and 3 x 4 against 4 x 3 (QPUs x qubits). Also planned: more seeds for QC against single-shot CC on permuted features, where QC wins by 2.4 +- 0.9 percentage points on only five seeds.
